> cc @whatwg/i18n @whatwg/a11y

on first reading, I don't have any accessibility concerns with this
It would be great if the explainer had some hints what the API might look like in the future so that it could support more languages.

I was [actioned](https://github.com/w3c/i18n-actions/issues/222) by the I18N WG with providing a response. Some discussion took place in the action item (details of which may be relevant to resolving our concerns). Here's the comment for posterity in this PR.

---

Implementing site- or page-specific custom dictionaries as a feature similar in concept to individual user dictionaries seems, at first, to be straightforward. It's simply a a word-token list used to suppress misspell hints/warnings by the user-agent. The list would be subject to the same sorts of normalization and string comparison issues inherent in any magical word list, but would require minimal effort to implement and would be no worse that the existing user dictionary feature.

There are potential issues with this if case or normalization sensitivity is considered. For more (way more than you desire) information, see [CharMod: String Matching](https://www.w3.org/TR/charmod-norm). See also [String Searching](https://www.w3.org/TR/string-search/) for some additional examples of dictionary-like processing and associated complications. The current design would require the custom dictionary to account for these types of string variation/permutation by adding multiple representations of the same string to the dictionary. This is fine if there is a single or small number of documents containing fairly static content. This is less good for a larger site, possibly evolving over time or dependent on content management systems.

There is also the problem that, for many languages, a simple word list may be inadequate due to the need to stem words ("run" vs. "ran"; "car" vs. "cars") or to add or remove affixes (such as the suffixes that are extremely common in Finnish). Lack of indication of the source language of the words stored in the dictionary removes the ability to do language-specific processing on the dictionary word (or on text when matching that word) for implementations that can make use of such information. Lack of a "slot" in the data structure might make it difficult to add such language metadata at a later time. We suggest including optional dictionary and word-level language metadata at both the storage and API level, even though no functionality is normatively attached initially (in the "simple list of words" era).

To which @r12a added:

There are a number of potential issues that i think should at least be considered and probably mentioned in the explainer and the spec.

1. i think it's probably essential to do character normalisation and case folding before comparing words
2. a simple character-by-character comparison quickly becomes unwieldy for users of many languages. For example:
    - languages using Chinese, Japanese, Thai, Khmer, etc scripts don't separate words with spaces, and so some kind of preprocessing will be needed to tokenise the text before comparison.  In some cases, this may lead to ambiguity as to what the appropriate segmentation is, especially when dealing with compound words.
    - languages like Finnish and Japanese pile prefixes and suffixes onto words to create complex meanings.  A single Inuit word can sometimes convey a whole sentence. Simple space-based segmentation may not take you far with spell-checkers for these languages.
    - other languages may ram small words into bigger ones in certain circumstances, such as the word 'and' in Arabic ('wa') is attached to the word that follows it, with no intervening space.
    - many languages, such as German and Russian - but also many more - heavily decline words according to the context, eg. spellings for the word 'book' in Russian include книга, книги, книг, книге, книгам, книгу, книгой, книгою, книгами, книгах. So rather than just creating a couple of entries 'book' and 'books', it's necessary for the user to provide many possible spellings for each word they want to add to the dictionary.  And that's just nouns — verbs also have many different forms. (Note also that languages like Russian and Arabic have more than one plural form for each word.)
    - Obviously some kind of integration of the dictionary mechanism with language-specific stemming will be necessary to extend the use to these languages.  (English is very unusual in its simplicity here.)
3. it appears that currently browsers use OS level language detection for spell checkers, rather than using the language set using the lang tag in HTML (for the page or for the input element). It seems that it could be more useful to allow for custom spell check dictionaries to be selected based on language detection or the lang attribute before falling back to system language settings.  Again, English speakers tend to be unusual in that they are often monolingual — much of the world outside of English-speaking regions is multilingual, and may need to check their spelling in more than one language, in a way that is context-dependent.

Whether or not the initial proposal takes these factors into account immediately, i think it should always be pointed out that these difficulties exist and will need to be addressed at some point. The solution implemented initially should provide (or at least not block) extension mechanisms that can later address non-Latin user requirements. We don't want the technology to be trapped in a situation that will only work for English.

---

We look forward to working with this group to resolve issues.

*This comment comes from the [Spoken Presentation (Pronunication) TF](https://www.w3.org/WAI/about/groups/task-forces/spoken-presentation/). We are excited to see this proposal, and have the following data, questions, and suggestions.*

**Our ask:** please can we include an IPA field as part of this, so that people (and later, ATs) will know how to pronounce the words?

**Background info:** The TF's goal is to develop normative specifications and guidance for author-controlled pronunciation across environments, including assistive technology (AT), as opposed to relying on platform heuristics.

There are some existing projects and work that may be of interest...

**Existing industry project:**

There is a significant project within the education assessment industry that uses data-ssml and JSON-encoded SSML to provide pronunciation.

1EdTech's data-ssml approach: <https://www.1edtech.org/standards/data-ssml>

This is an all-encompassing solution. We seek to create standards that would ultimately enable authors to achieve the parts of this solution that they need, in a simple, declarative way.

**Use Cases:**

There are significant use cases in education, including:

* Language learning and comprehension

* Historical pronunciations

We are still collecting use cases from our partners; draft document: <https://raw.githack.com/w3c/pronunciation/main/use-cases/index.html>

**Technical Gap Analysis:**

You can find the key part of our gap analysis comparing different technical approaches in our gap analysis document: <https://raw.githack.com/w3c/pronunciation/main/gap-analysis/index.html#gap-analysis>

Thanks @aphillips and @r12a. We've started addressing this in the explainer: https://github.com/Igalia/explainers/pull/117: 
  - **Normalization:** words are compared after NFC, so canonically equivalent spellings match.
  - **Case:** instead of case folding, we propose Unicode's default case mapping in one direction: a word also matches forms with more capitals, never fewer. "wolvic" accepts "Wolvic" and "WOLVIC", but "Paris" does not accept "paris". This matches Hunspell and Apple's built-in dictionaries, and keeps capitals that are part of a spelling (proper nouns, brand names, acronyms). Language-specific gaps are listed, with language-aware mapping as future work.
  - **Segmentation:** the dictionary doesn't segment text; it filters words the platform spell checker has already flagged. The explainer now lists where that falls short.
  
We'd appreciate your view on this. Thanks!

Here's a quick reaction to the commit message, without looking at the text yet.

> Case: instead of case folding, we propose Unicode's default case mapping in one direction: a word also matches forms with more capitals, never fewer. "wolvic" accepts "Wolvic" and "WOLVIC", but "Paris" does not accept "paris". This matches Hunspell and Apple's built-in dictionaries, and keeps capitals that are part of a spelling (proper nouns, brand names, acronyms). Language-specific gaps are listed, with language-aware mapping as future work.

This is probably a problem. It is certainly a problem for Turkic languages. This is illustrated in-depth here: https://www.w3.org/TR/charmod-norm/#caseMappingLanguageSensitivity. I think that listing language-specific gaps for future work is a mistake.

You also need to be aware that case fold (or map) and normalization interact with one-another. See: https://www.w3.org/TR/charmod-norm/#normalizationAndCasefold

I get what you're trying to do. You don't have to worry about tokenization, because the spell-checker has already done that work for you. I'm not sure, but you might still need segmentation for cases like Finnish affixes. As a result, you have little word tokens coming from the corpus. This is useful, because you can do a number of things to the string for the purposes of matching. I am uncomfortable that you're creating a feature that works well for Western European languages, is mostly fine or irrelevant for East Asian ones, but might be less useful or potentially riddled with issues for languages that are less-well represented by our respective groups.

Among the things you might want to do that occur to me without much thought:

- normalize East Asian widths (generally by mapping narrow to wide)
- possibly transliterating Japanese hiragana to katakana
- removing Unicode invisible formatting controls and variation selectors

I'm not sure, but you might still need some level of segmentation for cases such as Finnish affixes.

We met with @aphillips and laid out [a plan](https://gist.github.com/bkardell/dbb639842a571ec3e0e8cd49fa22208e) for approaching this. With the current updates we think the spec is ready for further review comments
